reference.source: ATLS / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine (critical care)
clinicalPearls: Anticipate systemic collapse when a compressed limb or torso is released, as reperfusion floods the circulation with potassium and other cell contents
Hyperkalaemia is the most immediately life-threatening consequence and can precipitate fatal arrhythmia at or shortly after extrication
Begin generous intravenous fluid resuscitation early, ideally before release of the crushed part, to protect the kidneys and dilute the metabolic load
Myoglobin released from damaged muscle causes pigment-induced acute kidney injury, often heralded by dark, tea-coloured urine
Monitor the electrocardiogram continuously for peaked T waves and other signs of hyperkalaemia during and after extrication
The crushed limb can develop compartment syndrome, so examine repeatedly for tense swelling and disproportionate pain
Correct hypovolaemia, acidosis, and electrolyte disturbance in parallel while maintaining a good urine output
reference.pathophysiology: Prolonged compression of muscle causes ischaemic and pressure necrosis (rhabdomyolysis). While compressed, the injury is largely contained, but on release reperfusion washes the accumulated intracellular contents into the systemic circulation. Potassium, myoglobin, phosphate, and organic acids surge, producing hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, and hypocalcaemia. Myoglobin precipitates in the renal tubules, and combined with hypovolaemia from fluid sequestration into damaged muscle, causes acute kidney injury. Massive fluid shifts and the release of vasoactive and inflammatory mediators can cause shock, while swelling within fascial compartments produces compartment syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Acute kidney injury from other causes
Hyperkalaemia from renal failure or other aetiology
Compartment syndrome without systemic crush features
Hypovolaemic or haemorrhagic shock from associated trauma
additionalInvestigations: Serum potassium and other electrolytes, including calcium and phosphate
Creatine kinase and myoglobin as markers of muscle breakdown
Renal function and urine output monitoring
Urinalysis showing pigment (dark urine positive for blood without red cells)
Electrocardiogram and continuous cardiac monitoring for hyperkalaemic changes
redFlags: Hyperkalaemia with electrocardiographic changes threatening fatal arrhythmia around the time of extrication
Progressive acute kidney injury with falling urine output and dark urine
Signs of compartment syndrome in the crushed limb requiring urgent assessment
Metabolic acidosis and haemodynamic instability on reperfusion
Sudden cardiovascular collapse immediately after release of the crushed part
reference.prognosis: Early and aggressive fluid resuscitation with prevention and treatment of hyperkalaemia and pigment nephropathy improves outcome. Untreated crush syndrome carries high mortality from arrhythmia and renal failure, though renal function often recovers with timely supportive care and dialysis where needed.
pitfalls: Delaying fluid resuscitation until after the limb is freed, when the potassium surge is already underway
Overlooking hyperkalaemia and failing to monitor the electrocardiogram during extrication
Missing evolving compartment syndrome in the injured limb
Under-resuscitating and allowing pigment nephropathy to progress
Attributing dark urine to visible blood rather than myoglobin
management: Begin generous intravenous fluid resuscitation early, ideally before release of the compressed part, to protect the kidneys and dilute the metabolic load

Anticipate and treat hyperkalaemia with cardiac-membrane stabilisation using calcium and potassium-shifting therapy with insulin-dextrose and salbutamol, and continuous ECG monitoring for peaked T waves
Consider urinary alkalinisation with sodium bicarbonate and maintenance of brisk diuresis to limit pigment (myoglobin) nephropathy
Provide renal replacement therapy for refractory hyperkalaemia, severe acidosis or established acute kidney injury
Assess the limb repeatedly for compartment syndrome and perform fasciotomy where indicated
Correct symptomatic hypocalcaemia and metabolic acidosis and treat shock with ongoing haemodynamic support
Manage in a critical care setting with a trauma multidisciplinary team
